title: How to Develop a Multi-Currency Expert Advisor with the AI Assistant in MetaTrader 5
text:
One Expert Advisor, several currency pairs, various trading strategies, and a unified risk management system. The task seems quite straightforward until you start looking into the details.
Let's imagine that an Expert Advisor buys both EURUSD and GBPUSD at the same time. Technically, these are two separate trades, but both depend on movements in the U.S. dollar. If the dollar starts to strengthen, losses could occur on both positions at once. So it is not enough to simply teach an Expert Advisor to trade multiple instruments — you need to account for the relationships between them, allocate risk, and manage the entire portfolio.
Developing such a system requires knowledge of MQL5, statistics, trading program architecture, and risk management. But do you really have to figure all this out on your own?
A New Era in Algorithmic Trading
Starting with
build 6060
, MetaTrader 5 and MetaEditor feature a built-in AI Assistant with support for the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Artificial intelligence can now not only help write code, but also compile it, fix errors, and test it. This makes it possible to approach the development of even fairly complex trading systems in a new way.
We will show you how to use these features to create a fully-fledged multi-currency Expert Advisor. Moreover, we will not set all the trading rules in advance — we will ask the AI to independently select several strategies, research them, combine them into a portfolio system, and test the result.
We'll walk through the entire development process: the actual prompts given to the assistant, its decisions, the errors encountered, the test results, and the time spent. Let's see how well AI can handle a complex task on its own and in what situations it will need our intervention.
That said, our goal is not to create a trading system that is guaranteed to be profitable. It is more important for us to get a working prototype, understand the capabilities of the new tool, and assess how much it can simplify the work of an algorithmic trader.
A Good Start
Let's start not by writing code, but by organizing our work. If we simply ask the AI to create a multi-currency Expert Advisor, it might come up with its own trading rules, choose the architecture, and make a number of decisions that we won't be happy with.
So let's agree on this right away: first, we will draw up a plan, discuss each subsequent step in advance and record all significant actions and results in the development log. Open MetaTrader 5, go to the chat section, and start a conversation with the AI Assistant. Our first request will be very brief.
Hi.

We need to write an Expert Advisor, but first we will prepare a plan. Each step must be discussed first and executed only after my approval.
After a few minutes of deliberation, we get the first response:
As we can see, the AI Assistant got right to work and presented a detailed, ready-to-use development plan. But we will tighten up our working procedures a bit so that we have a rigorous technical record of our work.
We will give the assistant the first set of instructions, and they are very detailed. You can draft them on your own, but it is much faster and better to write it using any modern AI model — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and so on.
First, we will discuss the procedure.

Starting with this message, keep a continuous log of all significant actions taken on the project. The log is necessary for the subsequent analysis of the work done to develop a trading system using the AI Assistant.


## 1. Log file

Create a file named `DEVELOPMENT_LOG.md` in the MQL5 project directory.

If the file already exists, read it and continue the log without deleting the previous entries.

Save the log directly to disk, not just in the conversation context.

## 2. What to document

Record each significant stage:

- Defining the task and clarifying requirements.
- Designing algorithms and architecture.
- Creating and modifying source code.
- Adding new features and modules.
- Compiling and debugging.
- Identifying and correcting logical errors.
- Running tests and analyzing results.
- Optimizing and improving performance.
- Changes to requirements and technical decisions made.

Do not record every minor action. Group related operations into logical stages.

## 3. Time tracking

For each stage, record the following:

- Stage number and name.
- Start time and end time.
- Duration in minutes and seconds.
- A brief description of the actions performed.
- Files created or modified.
- Problems encountered and how they were resolved.
- The result obtained.

Use your computer's local time, specifying the time zone.

Get the actual time from an available system source. Do not make up timestamps or durations.

If you cannot determine the exact time, enter "not measured." If the duration is an estimate, clearly indicate that it is an estimate.

Distinguish between:
- The total elapsed time of the stage, including wait time for compilation and testing.
- Active working time, only if it can actually be measured.

## 4. Logging guidelines

Before starting a new significant stage, write down its name, purpose, and start time.

Once the stage is complete, immediately update the log entry with the results and end time.

If an error occurs, document its cause, the correction made, and the result of the recheck.

If the stage is not complete, leave the status as IN PROGRESS. At the next startup, check for unfinished stages.

Do not delete records of failed attempts. They are valuable for a technical article.

If a fix proves unsuccessful, record that in the history rather than replacing the original result.

For each new user request, first check the status of the log and the open stage. After completing the request, update the log before reporting completion.

## 5. Log format

At the beginning of the file, maintain a summary containing:

- Project name.
- Development start date.
- Current status.
- Number of completed stages.
- Total measured time.
- Number of compilations, errors, and test runs, if these figures are reliably known.

For each stage, use the following structure:

### Stage N. title

- Start:
- End:
- Duration:
- Purpose:
- User Request: Brief Summary
- Actions:
- Files Modified:
- Errors and Corrections:
- Verification:
- Result:
- Status: DONE / IN PROGRESS / FAILED

## 6. Check before finalizing your response

Before each message reporting the completion of significant work:

1. Make sure the log is up to date.
2. Verify that actual compilation or test results are available if compilation or testing was performed.
3. Do not mark a task as successfully completed without first verifying it.
4. Briefly report the result and the log entry.

## 7. Final report

When I write "Prepare a development report," read through the entire log and prepare a brief technical report with the following sections:

1. What problem was being solved.
2. How the architecture and trading logic were developed.
3. The main stages of development in chronological order.
4. What errors occurred and how the AI Assistant corrected them.
5. How compilation, debugging, and testing were performed.
6. What results were obtained?
7. How long did the development take overall, and how long did each major stage take?
8. What limitations or unresolved issues remain?

Add a concise table listing the stages and their durations.

The report must be factual and free of promotional language. It will serve as the foundation for improving robot development processes on MQL5.com.

## 8. Instruction priority

Treat keeping the log as a permanent working rule for this project. It applies to all subsequent stages until my explicit instruction to disable logging.

If the dialog context is shortened or a new session starts, restore the work history from DEVELOPMENT_LOG.md.

Do not rely on your own memory instead of the saved file.

Now create the log, write the project start time, and confirm that the file was actually created on disk. If there is no access to the file system, say so directly.
The AI Assistant immediately creates a log and makes the first entries in it:
Choosing a Trading System
Modern models are vast encyclopedias covering virtually every field of knowledge. If we set clear rules for trading, we will, to some extent, limit our options. So let's ask the AI to come up with some ideas on its own—that will be a good starting point. Our goal is not to create a fully functional, profitable system on the first try, but to gain development experience and lay a solid foundation for future projects. Before AI was introduced in MetaTrader 5, this process could take days or even weeks of intensive programming in MetaEditor. Now we can do this right from the terminal, even if we have no experience with the development environment
We need to write an Expert Advisor that will trade using multiple trading strategies and multiple symbols simultaneously. 

Therefore, it must take into account the correlation between instruments, allocate risk, and automatically limit the portfolio's overall exposure. 
First, we need to choose our strategies. Suggest several systems based on different concepts so that trading signals are generated under different market conditions.  
It is possible — and even desirable — for them to open opposing positions on the same instrument.
Here is the answer:
All right. Before we dive in, there's one critical technical point that affects the entire architecture.
Important: Opposing positions on a single instrument
Hedging account
— you can hold both a Buy and a Sell position on the same symbol at the same time. The strategies actually overlap; net exposure is calculated as the sum.
Netting account
— the second, opposite position is not opened separately; it reduces or reverses the existing one. "Opposing positions on a single instrument" are technically impossible—only a net position is possible.
Please tell me what type of account is being used (or is planned). This determines whether we create a layer of "virtual" positions (accounting for strategies within a single net position) or use actual hedging.

S1 vs. S2
— opposite in nature: trend following captures continuation, while mean reversion captures pullbacks. On the same symbol, they provide a natural hedge across different market regimes.
S3

S6
uses correlation itself as a trading signal and works best in conjunction with portfolio exposure management (long one instrument / short a correlated one).
Recommendation for the first version
S1 + S2 + S6
— trend, mean reversion, and relative value. Three different market regimes, naturally opposing positions, and a direct connection to the correlation layer. S3/S4/S5 — planned for the second iteration to avoid bloating the first release.

Why not choose the purely statistical minimum (0.040)? That triplet — NZDUSD, EURGBP, and EURCHF — consists of instruments with similar characteristics: low volatility and predominantly range-bound markets. The trend-following strategy (S1) has no room to operate there, and the whole idea of "different market conditions" is lost.
The selected triplet offers three distinct market profiles with a maximum |corr| of 0.375 (compared to 0.8+ for the standard major currency pairs):
EURGBP
— low volatility, range-bound market → basis for S2 (mean reversion).
GBPJPY
— high volatility, strong trends → basis for S1 (trend breakout).
USDCAD
— moderate volatility, commodity-driven, almost uncorrelated with the other two.
Correlations are unstable over time: 0.375 reflects the current regime, not a constant. Therefore, a dynamic correlation layer will still be needed in the portfolio component; a static matrix is not sufficient.
An important implication for S6
Relative value, by definition, involves trading the spread between
correlated
instruments. The triplet is intentionally uncorrelated, so S6 will not be run on it. Options to choose from later:
add a fourth symbol (for example, a currency pair correlated with USDCAD) specifically for S6;
implement S6 as a synthetic spread (for example, EURGBP against the EURUSD/GBPUSD ratio);
replace S6 with another single-instrument strategy.
This is a decision for Stage 5; we will come back to it after S1/S2. I am just making a note of this so there will not be any surprises.

S1 Strategy Rules v1.0
Instrument:
GBPJPY.
Timeframe:
H1.
Indicators:
20-period Donchian channel (entry), 10-period Donchian channel (exit), ATR(14), ADX(14).
Entry
(once per bar, based on the closed bar; bar 0 is the current, unclosed bar):
Buy:
Close[1] > max(High[2..21]) AND ADX[1] ≥ 25
Sell:
Close[1] < min(Low[2..11]) … or, more precisely, min(Low[2..21]) AND ADX[1] ≥ 25
The channel is constructed using bars 2 through 21 — the signal bar is not included in its own breakout level.
No EMA filter is used (tested and found to be detrimental).
Exit:
Stop-loss:
2.0 × ATR[1] from the entry price; set immediately.
Take-profit:
None.
Reversal exit:
A long position is closed when Close[1] < min(Low[2..11]), and a short position is closed when Close[1] > max(High[2..11]).
Trailing stop:
optional, disabled by default; when enabled, the trailing distance is 1.5 × ATR, with an adjustment increment of 0.5 × ATR.
Position size:
Risk 0.5% of equity per trade.
lot = risk / ((SL distance / tick_size) × tick_value), rounded down to the nearest volume increment, subject to min/max limits.
One position per symbol+magic combination; no opposing positions are opened within S1.
Safety checks:
trading permissions for the terminal/account/Expert Advisor, symbol trading mode, stop level, freeze level when adjusting the trailing stop, and price normalization to the tick size.

The idea behind S2 is mean reversion
S2 trades against an overextended move in the absence of a trend: the price deviates from the local mean and is statistically likely to revert, while the ADX filter excludes instances where the deviation marks the start of a trend rather than noise.
The key difference from S1:
S1
S2
Market Conditions
trend, ADX ≥ 25
range-bound market, ADX < 20
Entry Direction
in the breakout direction
against the overextended move
Exit
on a channel reversal
on mean reversion
Characteristics
rare, large profits
frequent small profits
The ADX filters for these strategies are mutually exclusive — they should not generate signals simultaneously on the same instrument. This is precisely what leads to "opposing positions" during integration.
Methodology
The RegimeStatistics.mq5 script was written to calculate the following over 10,000 H1 bars: average ADX, the proportion of bars with ADX < 20, return autocorrelation (lag 1), variance ratio VR(2/5/10), efficiency ratio (10), ATR, and spread.
What the metrics mean:
VR < 1
— variance grows less than linearly, indicating mean reversion; VR > 1 indicates trending behavior.
Efficiency ratio
— the ratio of "net movement" to "distance traveled"; the lower the ratio, the more erratic and sideways the movement.
Proportion of time with ADX < 20
— how much time the instrument spends in a weak trend.

Why EURGBP
The most time spent in a range-bound market
— 23.3% of bars with ADX < 20, compared to 17–19.5% for the others. This is exactly the state in which S2 is permitted to operate.
The lowest efficiency ratio
(0.3073) indicates the least linear price movement; the price tends to retrace more often than it continues in the same direction.
The lowest VR(10)
= 0.911 — over a 10-hour horizon, deviations tend to diminish statistically.
Lowest volatility
— 0.068% of the price per hour. Mean reversion calls for a narrow, choppy range, not large price swings.
A cross pair without the dollar
— less dependence on the USD factor, which helps reduce correlation with S1 on GBPJPY.
Honest counterarguments
Trade Cost.
The EURGBP spread is 2 points with an ATR of 56.8 points, which is 3.5% of the ATR — the worst figure out of the four. For USDCAD, the spread is just 0.86% of ATR. This means the target should be at least ~0.5–1 ATR; otherwise, the spread will wipe out the edge. Frequent scalping on the EURGBP pair is not recommended.
USDCAD is no worse on some metrics:
its autocorrelation of −0.0435 and VR(5) of 0.916 are even stronger. However, it has a higher ER, spends less time in a range-bound market (with more trending episodes driven by oil prices and Bank of Canada meetings), and is reserved for S6.
Risk of event-driven gaps.
Political developments in the EU and UK can cause rare but wide gaps — an ATR-based stop may be subject to slippage.
A prolonged trend
(GBP under pressure) — a counter-trend strategy will result in mounting losses, so a strict stop-loss and an ADX filter are essential.
Proposed S2 specification (draft)
Instrument:
EURGBP.
Timeframe:
M15–H1, selected based on testing.
Signal:
z = (Close − SMA(20)) / StdDev(20).
Long: z[1] ≤ −2.0 and ADX(14)[1] < 20.
Short: z[1] ≥ +2.0 and ADX(14)[1] < 20.
Target:
SMA(20) at the time of entry (z → 0).
Stop:
2.0 × ATR(14) from the entry.
Time-based exit:
Close the position after N bars (24) if neither the target nor the stop-loss has been triggered.

Conclusion on S2: The edge has not been confirmed.
The timeframe acts as a transaction cost filter: M5 → M15 → M30 → H1 yield PF values of 0.42 → 0.70 → 0.91 → 1.10. The logic is simple: with an ATR of 56.8 points for EURGBP (H1) and a spread of ~2 points, any target smaller than 0.5×ATR is eaten up by the spread; on M5, there are 1,157 trades, and each one incurs an entry/exit cost.
H1 in the 2025–2026 sample is positive, but the 2023–2024 OOS is negative, and the full backtest yields a profit of +52 USD across 367 trades — this is noise, not an edge. The observation is the same as with S1: I won't tune the parameters to fit the profitable period, as that would lead to overfitting.
No parameter tuning was performed; a minimum target of 0.5 ATR served as protection against scalping, but this is only a reprieve, not an edge.

For all three symbols, the profit sign changes when the period changes: EURGBP and GBPJPY are positive in 2025–2026 and negative in 2023–2024, while for USDCAD, it is exactly the opposite (negative in the recent period, PF 1.33 in OOS). No instrument has the same profit sign across the two periods.

The hypothesis that "the idea works, but the instrument is unsuitable" was not confirmed: EURGBP, with its worse spread/ATR ratio, performed no worse than USDCAD, with its better ratio. So, it is not about the instrument or the timeframe, but about the logic itself: an entry at an extreme z-score on a closed bar does not provide enough of an edge to cover transaction costs.
To be clear about the limitations: these tests used the "open prices" model, with no slippage or commission; switching to real ticks is likely to worsen S2's results, since it trades frequently and against the price move.

Conclusion
On the H1 and H4 timeframes, φ = 0.9985–1.0001: the spread of the hedged ratio is essentially a random walk, with a half-life of 146 bars or more. Classic z-score-based relative value trading has no statistical basis on intraday timeframes.
Transaction costs are not to blame here: cost_to_sd ≤ 0.003 — the cost of the two legs is negligible relative to the variability of the spread. The limiting factor is the lack of mean reversion, not the cost.
On D1, mean reversion emerges, but the half-life is 106–604 days, implying holding periods of weeks and months; moreover, the correlation is unstable across the two halves (0.656 versus 0.807). This is a different product — a position-trading pair — outside the agreed M5–H1 range.
The decision not to create the S6 Expert Advisor was deliberate: not a single pair passed the filter, so writing it would have meant testing a design already known to be unworkable.
Errors found and corrected along the way
In version 1.00, the reversion metric was calculated as a sum without dividing by the number of observations and counted every bar in the episode, rather than only new threshold crossings — it yielded −13 sd (nonsense). Fixed: averaging across horizons + counting only transitions from outside the threshold to inside.
MathSign is not defined in MQL5 (undeclared identifier) and has been replaced with an explicit condition.
The check beta <= 0.05 rejected negatively correlated pairs (EURUSD/USDCHF); it was changed to use the absolute value of β.
For D1, there was no historical data for USDCHF/EURJPY/EURGBP/EURCHF/NZDUSD (CopyClose → −1) — I loaded the daily bars, and the measurements were completed.
To be transparent about an incident: when I overwrote SpreadScreening.mq5, I erased your manual edit (the MathSign replacement mentioned above). The edit has been explicitly restored, with no change in meaning.

judge.reject_reason: Статья не содержит полного детерминированного правила для проверки на закрытых барах спот-форекса. Хотя отдельные стратегии S1 и S2 описаны частично, они явно отвергнуты как неподтверждённые («statistical edge has not been confirmed», «S2 is closed», «S1 is suitable only as a portfolio component»), а интегрированное правило для мультивалютного EA — отсутствует. Нет ни единого условия входа, объединяющего сигналы, нет формулы или логики комбинирования стратегий, нет описания, как формируется итоговое направление сделки по портфелю. Указано лишь: «we will incorporate S1, S2, and S6 as if they were profitable», но конкретное правило — не приведено. Это фатальный порок: статья не про рабочее торговое правило, а про процесс разработки с использованием ИИ-ассистента.

judge.summary: Статья описывает процесс разработки мультивалютного эксперта с помощью встроенного ИИ-ассистента MetaTrader 5, включая выбор стратегий, анализ корреляций и бэктесты. Однако ни одна из предложенных стратегий (S1, S2, S6) не прошла валидацию, и интегрированное торговое правило для финального EA так и не сформулировано — автор останавливается на этапе принятия решения о продолжении разработки без предоставления рабочего правила.
